domain.title: The Level Itself
domain.tag: how Google levels work · the loop · what promotion actually measures
domain.why: Being technically excellent is necessary but not enough on its own to reach the most senior engineering levels — those are judged by how much impact your work has across an entire company, not just how much you personally know. This domain is honest about that: it's not a body of knowledge you can memorize your way through, it's a map of what kind of work and what kind of evidence actually opens those doors, so you can start building toward it early instead of discovering it too late.

Google   Meta  Amazon              Microsoft        typical YOE
L3       E3    SDE I               -                0-2
L4       E4    SDE II              -                2-5
L5       E5    SDE III             63/64            5-8    <- terminal
L6       E6    Sr SDE / PE-track   65/66            8-12
L7       E7    Principal (L7)      67/68            12-18
L8       E8    Sr Principal (L8)   69/70            15-20+
L9       E9    Distinguished (L10) Distinguished    18-25+
L10      E10   VP / Distinguished  Technical Fellow 20-30+

the YOE column is folk knowledge, not data
L0.cloze:
Google {{c1::L5}} = Meta E5 = Senior, and is the {{c2::terminal}}
level with no up-or-out above it. Staff is {{c3::L6}}/E6.
Distinguished is {{c4::L9}}/E9. The years-of-experience column is
{{c5::folk knowledge, not data}}.

concepts.L1: L3 entry, L4 SWE, L5 Senior, L6 Staff, L7 Senior Staff, L8 Principal, L9 Distinguished, L10 Fellow. L5 is the terminal level — no up-or-out above it.
concepts.L2: L6 is the first level where the assessment shifts from 'can you build it' to 'can you decide what should be built.' That shift, not additional technical depth, is what the promotion committee is looking for.
concepts.L3: Terminal means the company will keep you at L5 indefinitely; below it, failure to progress eventually ends the employment. That single property explains why the levels above behave differently: promotion past L5 is opt-in and competitive rather than expected, so the criteria stop describing competence and start describing scarcity. Be careful with the years column: every widely circulating years-per-level table traces back to content farms that cite nothing and recycle each other. What is genuinely published is the shape of the pyramid, the under-10-percent figure for Staff, and each company's own written definition of scope per rung.

L4.prompt_tpl: A recruiter offers you {lvl} and says it is 'equivalent to Staff'. Name the Google, Meta and Amazon labels that actually correspond, and state what evidence you should ask for instead of trusting the mapping.
L4.answer: Staff is Google L6, Meta E6, Amazon Senior SDE on the principal track. SDE III is Senior, one rung lower, so a claim that SDE III equals Staff is a downlevel dressed as an equivalence. Ask for the written scope definition for the level and the compensation band, not the label.
L4.explanation: Titles are not portable and companies exploit that. The ladder document and the band are the two things that mean the same thing everywhere, which is why Dropbox publishing its framework is unusually useful even if you never work there.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what 'terminal level' means at {co} and derive why the promotion criteria above it describe scarcity rather than competence.

co: a company with an up-or-out policy below Senior

L4.answer: Terminal means you can stay at Senior indefinitely with no up-or-out pressure. Because staying is permitted, promotion above it is optional and must be rationed, so the rubric shifts from 'is this person good enough' to 'is this a scope only a few people in the company hold' - a comparative judgement rather than an absolute one.
L4.explanation: This is why 'I got better' does not produce a promotion above Senior. The rubric compares you against a scarce category, not against a bar. It also explains the committee structure: rationing decisions need a body that sees many candidates at once.

concepts.t: L8 and L9 are not interview outcomes

L0.body:
what an L8/L9 external hire actually looks like:
  a named system the industry uses, or
  a body of published work with a citation trail, or
  a recognized public track record with people who will vouch

Google Fellows, observed pattern:
  most joined between 1999 and 2013
  recognized 12-25 years after joining
  PhDs common; Jeff Dean 1999, Sanjay Ghemawat 2000, Jouppi 2013

there is no loop. there is a search, and then a negotiation.
L0.cloze:
External hires at L8/L9 are driven by {{c1::public track record}},
not by an interview loop. Most Google Fellows joined between
{{c2::1999 and 2013}} and were recognized {{c3::12-25 years}} later.
There is no loop; there is a {{c4::search}}, and then a negotiation.

concepts.L1: External hires at these levels are rare and driven by public track record — recognized systems, papers, a name that carries weight. There is no loop to prepare for.
concepts.L2: The honest path is entering at L6 or L7 and being promoted on demonstrated impact. Anyone selling L9 interview prep is selling something that doesn't exist.
concepts.L3: The mechanism is that the level is a claim about industry-scale impact, and an interview cannot produce evidence of industry-scale impact. Interviews sample skill in a two-hour window; L8 and L9 require a record other people already know about. This is why the honest route is entry at L6 or L7 and internal promotion, and why anything selling L9 interview preparation is selling a stage that does not occur. The corollary for planning: the observed Fellow pattern is 15 to 25 years of tenure with a named body of work, so what an external candidate is assessed on at those levels was accumulated elsewhere, over a decade, usually in public.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are {y} years into your career and want to reach Distinguished. Choose between preparing harder for senior interview loops and spending the same hours on public technical work, and justify with what an L8/L9 external hire is assessed on.
L4.answer: Public work. Interview preparation raises the probability of entering at L6 rather than L5, which is worth something and is bounded. The L8/L9 decision is a search over people with a known public record, so the only input that can ever make you visible to that search is work someone outside your company can see.
L4.explanation: Both matter, at different times. Loop preparation has the shorter shelf life and a hard ceiling; public work compounds and is the only one that appears in the criteria for the level actually being targeted. The two are not in conflict on any single day, but they are in conflict over a year of hours.

L0.body:
the packet:
  self-assessment, written by you
  peer feedback, 4-8 people, weighted toward outside your team
  manager's case
  artifacts: design docs, launch results, incident writeups

scored on:
  scope       how many teams changed behaviour because of you
  complexity  ambiguity resolved, not difficulty overcome
  impact      outcomes attributable to your judgment

the committee never met you. they read the record only.
L0.cloze:
A packet is a {{c1::self-assessment}} plus peer feedback plus the
manager's case plus artifacts. It is scored on {{c2::scope}}, complexity
and impact, where scope means {{c3::how many teams changed behaviour
because of you}}. The committee {{c4::never met you}}.

concepts.L1: A packet of your own writing plus peer feedback, assessed on scope, complexity, and impact. Ambiguity resolved, cross-team influence, and outcomes attributable to your judgment.
concepts.L2: Scope means how many teams your decisions affected. Two engineers with identical technical output level differently based entirely on blast radius of influence, and that is a thing you can deliberately choose to increase.
concepts.L3: Scope is the only one of the three that you can move deliberately and quickly, because it is a property of which problem you pick rather than of how well you execute. Two engineers can ship identical code and land in different levels because one shipped it into a corner and the other shipped it into a dependency three teams now build on. The operational consequence is to choose work by blast radius before choosing it by interest, and to write it down where the affected teams will cite it. Peer feedback from outside your team converts blast radius into packet evidence, which is why the cross-team document beats the cross-team conversation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two engineers ship equally difficult systems. A's system is used by {a} team; B's by {b} teams and is a build dependency for {c} more. Using scope as the scored variable, rank them and state the ratio of their blast radii. Answer with the ratio of blast radii.
L4.answer: B's blast radius is b + c teams versus A's a. b=3,c=2 -> 5 vs 1, ratio 5. b=3,c=5 -> 8 vs 1, ratio 8. b=4,c=2 -> 6 vs 1, ratio 6. b=4,c=5 -> 9 vs 1, ratio 9. B ranks higher on scope in every case despite equal difficulty.
L4.explanation: Counting teams is crude and it is closer to what the rubric measures than any measure of difficulty. The practical use is at project selection time: if you can name only one team affected before you start, the packet will say so afterwards.

L4.prompt_tpl: You resolved a {n}-month ambiguity that three teams were blocked on, and produced very little code. Explain how to write that into a packet so the committee scores it, and name the failure mode if you do not.
L4.answer: Write it as a decision with named alternatives, the evidence that selected one, the teams unblocked, and the dated document they now cite. The failure mode is the committee reading low code output and concluding no impact yet - Reilly's exact quote about glue work: 'You're not producing much code. You didn't have any impact yet.'
L4.explanation: Complexity in the rubric means ambiguity resolved, not difficulty overcome, so this work scores well when it is written as a decision and badly when it is written as coordination. The artifact is what makes the difference legible to people who were not there.

L0.body:
external offer expectation, strong staff-equivalent candidate:
  L6 / E6      default target
  L7 / E7      needs demonstrated multi-org technical leadership
               plus a referral advocating for the level
  L5 / E5      the common actual outcome ("downlevel")

what moves the level up, in order of effect:
  1. an internal advocate who states the level before the loop
  2. one design round with real depth, not uniform breadth
  3. a public artifact the interviewers have already seen

Larson: 1/3 of staff-plus engineers changed companies for the title
L0.cloze:
The default external target for a strong staff-equivalent candidate
is {{c1::L6}}/E6; {{c2::L7}} needs multi-org leadership plus a referral.
{{c3::Downlevelling}} is the common outcome when the loop is merely good.
About {{c4::one third}} of staff-plus engineers changed companies for the
title.

concepts.L1: L6 for a strong staff-equivalent candidate. L7 with demonstrated multi-org technical leadership and usually a referral advocating for the level.
concepts.L2: Downleveling is common and is the default outcome when the loop is merely good. The counter is depth demonstrated concretely in the design interview plus a strong internal advocate.
concepts.L3: Downlevelling is a default, not a punishment: committees resolve uncertainty downward because the cost of a wrong high level is visible and the cost of a wrong low level is not. The two counters are asymmetric in effort. An internal advocate who names the target level before the loop costs one relationship and moves the prior; a design round with genuine depth costs months of preparation and moves the evidence. Do both, in that order. Larson's survey gives the other half: two-thirds got staff-plus by internal promotion, one-third had to change companies, and about half the women surveyed had to. If internal promotion is blocked, switching is a documented route, not an admission of failure.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are targeting {lvl} externally and have {w} weeks. Allocate them between design-round depth, a referral who will advocate for the level, and a publishable artifact. Justify the allocation.
L4.answer: Spend the first week securing the referral, since it is cheap and sets the level before evaluation begins. Spend most of the rest on design-round depth, which is the highest-weighted round at senior levels. The artifact only pays off if it already exists or is nearly done, because it will not be finished and noticed inside the window.
L4.explanation: The ordering follows cost and timing. The referral is a small action with a large effect on the prior, and it must happen first to matter. Depth in the design round is the differentiator the loop actually scores. The artifact is a long-horizon investment mispriced as a short-horizon one.

L0.body:
Dropbox IC7 (Sr. Principal), verbatim from the public framework:
  Scope:     "I own and deliver company-wide product or platform goals
              with multi-year, multi-team effect"
  Influence: "I typically influence EPD and company-wide strategy to
              achieve business-impacting goals."

levels.fyi framework, verbatim:
  Staff:         "usually make up less than 10% of the company"
  Distinguished: impact "spans across the company and sometimes
                 industry"; "frequently published authors"
L0.cloze:
Dropbox IC7 Scope: "I own and deliver {{c1::company-wide}} product or
platform goals with {{c2::multi-year, multi-team}} effect."

levels.fyi: Staff engineers "usually make up {{c3::less than 10%}} of the
company." Distinguished impact "spans across the company and sometimes
{{c4::industry}}".

concepts.L1: Dropbox publishes its full engineering ladder, so you can read a company's own promotion language instead of a blogger's summary. IC7 is defined by three sentences about scope, influence and impact, and every one of them is a statement about organisations.
concepts.L2: Every noun in those definitions is a unit of organisation: company-wide, multi-year, multi-team, EPD strategy. Not one clause is about knowing more things. There is no curriculum whose completion satisfies a phrase that contains a time constant you cannot compress and a headcount you do not control.
concepts.L3: Map the rungs and the pattern holds across companies: Senior is L5/E5/SDE III, Staff is L6/E6, Senior Staff or Principal is L7/E7, Principal or Distinguished is L8/E8, Distinguished is L9/E9, Fellow is L10/E10. levels.fyi's framework is the only published population figure anywhere in this space: Staff is under 10 percent of a company. Nothing above that is published by anyone. The usual claim that each rung is roughly an order of magnitude scarcer gives Principal around 1 percent and Distinguished around 0.1 percent, but that is inference, not data, and anyone quoting you an exact headcount for L9 is guessing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Quote the Dropbox IC7 scope line from memory and name the {n} organisational quantities it requires. Then state what fraction of that line is a claim about technical knowledge.
L4.answer: "I own and deliver company-wide product or platform goals with multi-year, multi-team effect." The three organisational quantities are breadth (company-wide), duration (multi-year), and headcount (multi-team). None of the line is a claim about technical knowledge.
L4.explanation: The point of doing this from memory is that the line is short enough to hold and specific enough to plan against. Once you can recite it you stop treating a reading list as progress toward IC7, because you can see that the sentence contains no term a reading list moves.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineering org has {E} engineers. Using the one published figure (Staff is under 10 percent of the company) and the common assumption that each rung above Staff is roughly an order of magnitude scarcer, estimate the Staff, Principal and Distinguished headcounts, and state which of the three numbers is actually sourced. Answer with the Staff headcount.
L4.answer: Staff ~ 0.10E, Principal ~ 0.01E, Distinguished ~ 0.001E. E=30000 -> 3000 / 300 / 30. E=8000 -> 800 / 80 / 8. E=1200 -> 120 / 12 / 1.2. Only the Staff figure is sourced; the other two are inference from an unverified order-of-magnitude assumption.
L4.explanation: levels.fyi publishes the under-10-percent figure for Staff. No major company publishes level population counts at all, so the Principal and Distinguished numbers here are a modelling assumption. The useful takeaway is the shape: at 1200 engineers the model predicts roughly one Distinguished engineer, which is why small companies have no L9 problems to solve.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two candidates for promotion to {level}. A shipped a technically harder system alone. B shipped a simpler system that three other teams adopted and now depend on. Who levels higher under the published ladder language, and which exact phrase decides it?
L4.answer: B. The deciding phrase is 'multi-year, multi-team effect' in the Dropbox scope line, and its equivalent in every other ladder. Technical difficulty appears nowhere in the definition; number of teams affected appears in it directly.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common misreading of a ladder. Difficulty is a property of the work; scope is a property of the blast radius. The rubric scores the second. A is not being punished for depth, but depth only converts into level when other teams' outcomes depend on it.

concepts.t: Scope, not knowledge breadth, is the promoted variable

L0.body:
level ~= f(scope of problems owned,
           organizational recognition,
           sponsor seniority,
           years of visible track record)

knowledge  ->  a prerequisite filter, not a term in f

Peterman (Meta): "Scope Is King... the scope of your work is what is
  most likely to influence their guess" [at your level]
Larson: "A Staff engineer isn't a better Senior engineer, but someone
  who's moved into fulfilling one of the Staff archetypes."
Larson: "Being a Staff-engineer is... the intersection of the role,
  your behaviors, your impact, and the organization's recognition.
L0.cloze:
level ~= f({{c1::scope of problems owned}},
           organizational recognition,
           {{c2::sponsor seniority}},
           years of visible track record)

Knowledge is a {{c3::prerequisite filter}}, not a term in f.

Larson: "A Staff engineer isn't a {{c4::better Senior engineer}}, but
someone who's moved into fulfilling one of the Staff archetypes.

concepts.L1: Across every first-hand account of staff-plus promotion, the scored variables are scope, judgment under ambiguity, and organisational recognition. Breadth of knowledge appears in none of them. It is a gate you pass once, not a dial the committee reads.
concepts.L2: This inverts how most people study. A programme that maximises knowledge acquired is optimising a variable the committee does not score, while the variable it does score is largely set by which problems your employer has and lets you own. Studying harder cannot raise a term that is not in the function.
concepts.L3: Larson's framing is the sharpest version: Staff is a different job, not the same job done better, so 'get better at engineering' is not a path to it. The archetypes only exist at certain company sizes, which means the ceiling on your level is partly set by your employer, not by you. What this actually implies for study is narrow and useful: study to clear the filter, then spend the marginal hour on the things that produce scope - owning a problem end to end, writing the document others execute, and picking an employer with problems big enough to have a Staff-shaped hole in them. There is no L9 problem at a forty-person startup.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {h} spare hours this quarter. Option A: work through {n} more textbooks in adjacent subfields. Option B: take ownership of one cross-team problem nobody owns and write the document that resolves it. Under the promotion function, which one moves your level, and what does the other one actually buy?
L4.answer: B moves level, because it adds scope and organisational recognition, both terms in the function. A buys nothing on the level axis directly; it raises the probability you can hold scope competently when you get it, which is real but is a filter effect, not a scored term.
L4.explanation: The honest version of this is not 'stop studying'. It is that study is instrumental: it makes you able to take the scope. If you already clear the technical bar for the problems available to you, more breadth has close to zero marginal effect on level and a large opportunity cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two engineers at {co} produce identical technical output this year. One is promoted, one is not. Using the promotion function, name the term that differed and describe how it is measured in a packet.
L4.answer: Scope, measured as blast radius: how many teams changed what they do because of the decision. In a packet it shows up as named teams, named dependencies, and peer feedback from outside the author's own team - not as lines of code or system complexity.
L4.explanation: Blast radius is the thing you can deliberately increase without working more hours: choose problems whose resolution other teams are waiting on, and write the resolution down where they can adopt it. The packet is evidence of that, which is why cross-team peer feedback carries disproportionate weight.

L0.body:
milestone                     duration     evidence
employable competence, new    6 wk - 6 mo  Ziegler ~6 wk (elite start);
  domain                                   80k floor 200 h; MATS 12 wk
strong senior, owns a system  4-8 yr       ladder folk data [thin]
staff-plus (L6/E6+)           8-12 yr      "luck, timing, and work";
                                           1/3 switched companies
distinguished (L9/E9)         15-25 yr     Google Fellows joined
                                           1999-2013

row 1 compresses under intensity. rows 2-4 do not.

concepts.L1: Four different milestones get collapsed into one word, career, and they run on different clocks. Skill acquisition responds to intensity and lands in weeks or months. Level does not, because level contains a track-record term and a recognition term.
concepts.L2: The compressible row is the only one people quote. Ziegler's six weeks are real and are also the six weeks of an MIT computer science graduate who had started a Stanford PhD, retargeting existing elite ability. The floor 80,000 Hours gives a less-prepared starter is at minimum 200 hours, and likely more.
concepts.L3: Why the bottom three rows resist compression: each contains terms that require other people to observe you over calendar time. Dropbox IC7 asks for multi-year, multi-team effect, so at month 36 of a perfect start you have roughly one such cycle of evidence against a level that asks for a portfolio of them. Google's Fellows joined between 1999 and 2013 and were recognised 12 to 25 years later. Macnamara's meta-analysis of 88 studies puts deliberate practice at 12 percent of performance variance overall and under 1 percent, not statistically significant, in professions - partly a measurement artifact, but not evidence that hours alone produce elite professional standing.

L4.prompt_tpl: You begin full-time in {start}. Using the 15-25 year band for Distinguished, give the earliest and latest calendar years the level becomes plausible, and state the one condition that can make both numbers infinite. Answer with the earliest plausible year.
L4.answer: start + 15 to start + 25. 2026 -> 2041 to 2051. 2027 -> 2042 to 2052. Both are infinite if you never work at a company that has company-scale problems, because the level is defined by scope the employer must supply.
L4.explanation: The arithmetic is trivial and that is the point: it converts an aspiration into two dates you can look at. The condition matters more than the dates. Distinguished is a recognition of company-scale impact, so an employer without company-scale problems has no rung to promote you into, no matter how many years pass.

L4.prompt_tpl: At {h} focused hours per day, how many calendar days does the {F}-hour floor for a domain transition take, and how does that compare with the 500-600 hour block that a full quarter of this kind of work represents? Answer with the number of calendar days.
L4.answer: days = F / h. h=12: 200 h -> 16.7 d, 500 h -> 41.7 d, 600 h -> 50 d. h=8: 200 h -> 25 d, 500 h -> 62.5 d, 600 h -> 75 d. A 500-600 hour quarter is roughly 2.5-3x the 80,000 Hours floor and about 2-3x the hours in Ziegler's six weeks.
L4.explanation: This is the honest good news in the dossier. On the only clock that compresses, twelve hours a day for a quarter is a serious block - several times the stated minimum. It buys competence and artifacts. It does not buy a rung, because rungs are on the other three clocks.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone tells you a {m}-month programme will make you a Distinguished Engineer. Name which of the four clocks they are implicitly claiming to compress, and give the single sentence from a published ladder that refutes it.
L4.answer: They are claiming to compress the fourth clock using the mechanism of the first. The refutation is the Dropbox IC7 scope line: 'I own and deliver company-wide product or platform goals with multi-year, multi-team effect.' A multi-year effect cannot be evidenced inside a programme shorter than multiple years.
L4.explanation: The claim is not merely optimistic, it is category error: it treats a recognition level as a skill level. Notice the refutation is a quote from a company's own framework rather than an opinion, which is why this is the useful thing to memorise.

concepts.L1: Checked against the companies' own boards rather than commentary: the frontier labs have no India-based research or research-engineering roles. What does exist in India is Google Research India and MSR India in Bengaluru, and a very large NVIDIA silicon and AI presence.
concepts.L2: The uncomfortable consequence is that relocation is a variable in the plan, not an afterthought. The two remote-accessible on-ramps, MATS and the Anthropic Fellows Program, both ultimately feed roles located in San Francisco and London, so a visa route is part of the frontier-lab path from India whether or not you enjoy that.
concepts.L3: Stack this on Larson's finding that headquarters staff get more visibility than distributed offices and the problem compounds: the L8 and L9 scope problems are defined at headquarters, and the committee reads a record assembled by people in the room. Three honest strategies follow. Build a public reputation that routes around internal visibility, the only one fully under your control. Or relocate, via the H-1B lottery, UK Global Talent, or an intra-company transfer. concepts.L1: Every documented fast progression in the evidence base shares the same four inputs. None of the four is comprehensive knowledge, and two of them are things you join rather than things you study.
concepts.L2: Software can supply the first two and cannot supply the last two. A curriculum can build foundation and can structure full-time hours; it cannot assign you a senior mentor or place you in an environment where an artifact is the default output. A programme of solitary study is missing half of what every outlier had.
concepts.L3: The fine print on Ziegler is the part people skip. The guide documenting his six weeks states its assumed starting point: a technical bachelor's degree plus software engineering strong enough to pass a Google interview. Those six weeks were an elite engineer retargeting existing ability, not a novice arriving. The same guide's floor for a less-prepared starter is at minimum 200 hours, and likely more. Olah's nine years between dropping out and Anthropic is the other correction: the no-degree story is real and it is not a fast story. Operationally, inputs three and four are the ones to go buy - a fellowship, a repository, a community with review - because they are the two you are missing.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have inputs (1) and (2) and are working {h} hours a day for {d} days. Compute total hours and the multiple over the 200-hour floor, then state which of the four inputs that number does not address. Answer with the multiple over the 200-hour floor.
L4.answer: hours = h*d; multiple = hours/200. h=12,d=90 -> 1080 h, 5.4x. h=12,d=60 -> 720 h, 3.6x. h=10,d=90 -> 900 h, 4.5x. h=10,d=60 -> 600 h, 3.0x. The number addresses input (2) only; it says nothing about (3) a named mentor or (4) an artifact-producing environment.
L4.explanation: This is the useful and uncomfortable calculation. Even a very large hour count moves exactly one of the four inputs. Hours are the variable most under your control and the one with the least remaining headroom, which is why an application to a mentored programme is usually worth more than another hundred hours of study.

L4.prompt_tpl: You can add exactly one thing to a solitary study plan: {a}, a paid mentor for an hour a week, or membership in an open-source project with code review. Which input does each supply, and which do you add first?
L4.answer: More hours supplies input (2), which you already have. The mentor supplies (3). The open-source project supplies (3) and (4) at once, since review is feedback and merged work is a public artifact by default. Add the project first; it is the only option that buys two of the four missing inputs.
L4.explanation: The ranking falls out of the table rather than from taste. Note that the project is also free and requires no selection process, which makes it the highest expected value action available on any day you are not writing a fellowship application.

concepts.t: Reproducing a hard result as a portfolio strategy

L0.body:
modded-nanogpt speedrun (KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt)
  task:     train a 124M GPT to val loss 3.28 or below on
            FineWeb, 8x H100, as fast as possible
  baseline: Karpathy's llm.c GPT-2 replication, 45 min
  record:   1.353 min (29 Apr 2026); 82 records since May
            2024, each attributed to a named contributor
  rules:    data pipeline fixed; algorithmic and systems
            changes allowed; records hold at p<0.01
  spillover: the Muon optimizer came out of this arena

Ziegler: 5+ algorithms reimplemented, 2-10 days each (DQN, A2C,
  PPO, DDPG) on Gym, Cartpole to Atari
L0.cloze:
The speedrun target is val loss {{c1::3.28 or below}} on FineWeb with
{{c2::8x H100}}, against a {{c3::45 minute}} llm.c baseline; the record is
{{c4::1.353}} minutes over {{c5::82}} attributed records. Ziegler
reimplemented 5+ algorithms at {{c6::2-10 days}} each.

concepts.L1: Pick a published result with a stated number, reproduce it exactly, then change one thing and measure the difference. This is the cheapest artifact that is legible to a stranger, because the baseline does the explaining for you.
concepts.L2: The objection is that reproduction is not real work. Reproduction is where the unstated details live: the initialisation, the schedule, the numerical detail the paper omitted. A failed reproduction, documented well enough that a reader can locate the disagreement, is a genuine result and cheaper than a novel one.
concepts.L3: What makes an arena like the speedrun valuable is that it removes every ambiguity a hiring reader would otherwise have to resolve. The task is fixed, the hardware is fixed, the metric is a single number, records are attributed by name, and improvements must be statistically significant. Your contribution is unarguable in a way that no project description can be. Ziegler used the same principle without an arena: 20-30 deep-RL papers at roughly 1.5 hours each, then five or more algorithms reimplemented at 2-10 days apiece, sometimes twelve hours a day debugging and tuning. Debugging was the activity, not reading. Olsson's rule again: rather than learn X, try to learn to do X.

L4.prompt_tpl: Following Ziegler's method you reimplement {n} algorithms at {lo} to {hi} days each, working full-time. Give the calendar range in days and in weeks, and say what the range depends on. Answer with the upper end of the range in days.
L4.answer: days = n*lo to n*hi. n=5 -> 10 to 50 days, 1.4 to 7.1 weeks. n=7 -> 14 to 70 days, 2.0 to 10.0 weeks. The range depends almost entirely on debugging time, not on reading or typing time, which is why the spread is 5x.
L4.explanation: The 5x spread is the informative part. Implementation is fast and getting a wrong implementation to reveal that it is wrong is slow, so plan against the upper end. Ziegler's own description of the period was debugging and tuning, sometimes twelve hours a day.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {w} weeks for one portfolio artifact. Choose between building a novel system nobody has built, reproducing a published result and beating one number, and entering a public benchmark arena with attributed records. Justify by what a reader can verify.
L4.answer: The arena, then the reproduction, then the novel system. The arena has a fixed task, a fixed metric and named attribution, so a reader verifies your contribution in seconds. A reproduction needs the reader to trust your baseline. A novel system requires them to evaluate both the problem and the solution, which is expensive and usually is not done.
L4.explanation: Optimise for cheapness of verification, not for ambition. The novel system may be better work and it is worse evidence, because evidence is a property of the reader's cost to check. That asymmetry is why competitive public arenas are disproportionately effective for people without institutional credentials.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your reproduction lands at {loss} instead of the paper's number and you have checked it {k} times. Explain why this is publishable and what the write-up must contain for it to be a credential rather than a complaint.
L4.answer: It is publishable because a documented discrepancy is a result: either the paper omitted something or you did, and both are useful to readers. The write-up needs the exact configuration, the commit, the hardware, every difference from the paper you are aware of, the measurement variance across runs, and a specific hypothesis for the gap.
L4.explanation: The difference between a credential and a complaint is whether a reader can act on it. Variance across repeated runs is the item people omit and the first thing a careful reader asks for, because a single run cannot distinguish a real gap from noise.

prereqs: Public research output as the strongest available credential

concepts.t: Open source as a hiring funnel

L0.body:
EleutherAI paper (arXiv 2210.06413), verbatim:
  "The early members of EleutherAI were largely not from the ML or
   NLP academic communities, but consisted mostly of software
   engineers, ML hobbyists, and researchers in fields outside of
   machine learning"
  "individuals with minimal computer science backgrounds and no
   prior research knowledge becoming core contributors... within a
   matter of weeks"
  compute: donated allocations (CoreWeave, TPU Research Cloud)

where to work: GPU MODE, vLLM, torchtitan, TransformerLens, GPT-NeoX
quarter target: 2-4 merged PRs in a real repository
L0.cloze:
EleutherAI's members were "mostly {{c1::software engineers, ML
hobbyists, and researchers in fields outside of machine learning}}", and
some became core contributors "within {{c2::a matter of weeks}}". Compute
came from {{c3::donated allocations}}. A quarter's target is
{{c4::2-4 merged PRs}} in a real repository.

concepts.L1: A merged pull request in a live repository is a third-party endorsement: a maintainer with reputation staked on the project read your code and accepted it. That is evidence no course or certificate can produce.
concepts.L2: The misconception is that you need permission or an invitation. The bar is a reviewed diff, and the first useful contributions are usually failing tests, reproductions of open issues, and documentation of behaviour the maintainers already know is undocumented. Nobody is waiting to grant access.
concepts.L3: The EleutherAI paper is the strongest primary evidence that non-credentialed open work produces real researchers, and it also names the mechanism: members could draw on donated GPU allocations, so the compute barrier is surmountable without an employer. Kernel work is the most self-evidencing corner of this - a kernel that beats a cuBLAS or PyTorch baseline on a stated benchmark needs no reference letter. One honest caveat: GPU MODE publishes no membership figures and no documented hiring outcomes, so treat it as a place to do the work rather than as evidence that the work gets hired. The funnel is real; its conversion rate is unmeasured.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have {w} weeks and want your first merged PR in a large inference or training repository. Choose your first contribution among a new feature, a failing-test reproduction of an open issue, and a refactor you think improves the design. Justify by review cost.
L4.answer: The failing-test reproduction. It is small, it is obviously useful, it requires no design agreement, and a maintainer can review it in minutes. A feature needs buy-in you have not earned; an unsolicited refactor is the highest-review-cost, lowest-trust contribution a newcomer can open and is usually declined.
L4.explanation: Maintainer attention is the scarce resource, so the contribution that wins is the one cheapest to review and hardest to argue with. This is also why the first merge matters more than its size - it converts you from a stranger into someone whose next patch gets read.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why {n} merged pull requests in a real repository is stronger hiring evidence than a certificate for the same subject, in terms of who did the verifying.
L4.answer: A certificate says an institution verified you against a syllabus it also wrote. A merged PR says a practitioner with their own reputation at stake read your specific code, in their codebase, and accepted the risk of it running in production. The second is adversarial verification by someone with something to lose.
L4.explanation: Anthropic's careers page asks applicants to put independent research, blog posts and open source at the top of the resume, and lists no certifications anywhere. That is the same reasoning stated from the hiring side: they want evidence verified by someone whose incentives were not aligned with passing you.
